desc:
Bars of width 1 stand in a row with heights heights[i]. The floor area of a block of consecutive bars is the height of its shortest bar multiplied by the number of bars in the block (the largest rectangle that fits in the block along its full length).

Given an integer k, return the largest number of bars in a block whose floor area is at least k. If no block qualifies, return 0.

Example: heights = [6, 5, 6, 5, 1, 7] and k = 20. The first four bars have floor area 5 * 4 = 20, so the answer is 4. No block of 5 bars qualifies because it would contain the bar of height 1 or fewer than five good bars.
hints: Checking every block is O(n<sup>2</sup>) (or O(n<sup>3</sup>) if you recompute minima). Which blocks are worth looking at?
If a block has minimum m and length t, extend it as far as possible while all bars stay at least m. The floor area does not decrease and the length does not shrink.

So only the maximal blocks around each bar (bounded by the nearest strictly shorter bars) matter: take every bar with height * reach_width ≥ k and return the largest such width. Find the widths with a monotonic stack.
editorial: Suppose a block has minimum height m and length t with m * t ≥ k. Take a bar of height m inside it and widen the block to the largest block around that bar in which all bars are at least m, with width w ≥ t. Its floor area is at least m * w ≥ m * t ≥ k, so it also qualifies and is not shorter. Hence the answer is the maximum width w of such a maximal block over all bars with height * w ≥ k.

Conversely, such a maximal block of width w has minimum at least the bar's height, so its floor area is at least height * w ≥ k, i.e. it really qualifies. Compute the widths for all bars with the nearest-strictly-shorter-bar stack passes, then take the maximum over qualifying bars (0 if none). Time O(n), space O(n).
